title: C pointers: why +1 doesn't mean +1 byte
description:
Adding 1 to a pointer in C does not add one byte. The compiler scales it by the size of the pointed-to type, which is exactly why nums[i] equals *(nums + i). The same lesson also explains why arrays are not pointers: pass one into a function and its size collapses from 40 bytes to 8. Watch to see both in action.

Source lesson(s):
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-2/01-pointers-deep-dive/

#Shorts

beats.narration: Here's a C question. Add one to an int pointer. How far does the address move? Not one byte. A whole element.
The compiler knows the type. Add one to an int pointer, it jumps by sizeof int. The same step on a char pointer moves one byte.
Same plus one, a different jump each time, four bytes versus one. It's also why nums index i is just star of nums plus i.
Pass an array into a function and the size info vanishes. Inside it's only a pointer, so forty bytes reads as eight.
So arrays are not pointers. They decay the moment you pass them, and the length is gone. That's why array functions always want a count.
The full deep dive covers const placement, void star, and function pointers.
